item.title: How Locus Robotics is getting a grasp on one of robotics biggest challenges: manipulation
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Locus Robotics recently acquired Nexera Robotics, which create unique soft picking technology, bolstering its manipulation capabilities.

The post How Locus Robotics is getting a grasp on one of robotics biggest challenges: manipulation appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
NeuraGrasp can grasp a wide range of items, from small containers to porous polybags and cloth items. | Source: Locus Robotics

Locus Robotics Corp. has successfully tackled many robotic challenges in real working environments. Its autonomous mobile robots, or AMRs, have navigated countless miles in a variety of facilities, and they have aided in more than eight billion picks. Now, its targeting manipulation.

The company entered the robotic picking space in March 2025 when it unveiled Locus Array, a mobile manipulator equipped with a custom-developed, vision-guided picking arm. Over a year later, Locus acquired Nexera Robotics, which is known for its NeuraGrasp gripping technology.

According to Roy Belak, the senior vice president of robotic grasping at Locus and former CEO of Nexera, by the time it came in contact with Locus, Nexera had already spent years refining its unique, soft end effectors. It had already gone through at least six different product generations, he said.

“Just as we were getting to that point where the technology was showing its compelling capabilities, we were at a fortuitous situation where we met with Locus at MODEX, and I think the history kind of writes itself from there,” Belak told The Robot Report.

The timing was ideal for both companies. Locus wanted to be able to handle more SKUs in its facilities, and Vancouver, Canada-based Nexera was ready to scale.

“We want to see this technology deployed at scale,” said Belak. “That’s something that excites me as somebody who’s an innovator and building something. You just want to see it out there widely, and that seemed like it was a great opportunity.”

What does NeuraGrasp bring to Locus Array?

Nexera met Locus in 2025, when Locus was planning its early market release for Array. At the time, Array had a standard suction-cup gripper. Belak said the companies spent a lot of time figuring out how to fit Nexera’s technology into Array’s development so late in the game.

Luckily, even though Locus was already far into its process of developing Array, the robot was already well prepared for Nexera’s technology. Array already had an air supply, a power supply, and other things that Nexera’s technology needed.

“There was a lot of work that was done prior to the acquisition to make sure the technology could be slipped into the development stream,” recalled Belak. “I think it we had missed that window by another year, it probably would have been really hard to make those changes.”

While Belak did not give an exact timeline of when customers could gain access to Nexera’s technology, he said he is optimistic about the process. Belak said he expects that the next time Array is displayed publicly, it will likely have Nexera technology.

Right now, Locus is in the early stages of deploying Array with its original gripper to customers, so Nexera hasn’t seen the windfall of data that will be coming soon.

“There’s a long line of customers with their hands up that are really excited about Array,” Belak said. It’s in some ways intimidating, because you’re going to take this thing, you’re going to integrate it, and then it’s  going to go to many different places. Then we’ll start seeing the data really come back, and we’ll have a chance to just optimize as much as we can during that process.”

Suction versus pinch picking

When taking a step back and looking at the robotics industry as a whole, Belak said that much of robotic manipulation falls on a spectrum between suction-based grasping and pinch grasping.

“The reality is that suction is very good, particularly in warehouse operations,” he said. “Sixty percent to 70% of the time, it’s all you need. It’s when you get to that 30% to 40% and get to the really high coverage ratios.”

NeuraGrasp’s soft gripping technology can help to bridge this gap because it uses both suction and pinching, according to Belak.

“As an industry trend, it’s 100% recognized that pinch grasping is likely going to be very influential in the future of robotic grasping,” he said. “With that said, we are still firm believers that suction gets you a good portion of the way with air. And if it ain’t broke, you don’t throw it away.”

Locus is focusing on reliability and quality picks, not speed

“In the industrial environment, reliability is everything,” Belak said. “Suction technologies, although they have a performance limitation, the beauty of them is that they’re incredibly reliable. As we go to pinch grasping technologies, depending on the level of complexity that’s there, they can border on marginally reliable to very unreliable, or maybe just questionably reliable.”

Belak said it’s important to make robots that can simply do tasks successfully. But after that, the top priority is reliability, because it doesn’t matter how well a robot can pick if it’s constantly breaking down or missing picks. In addition, the quality of the pick is essential, he said.

“There’s a big differentiation between being able to do something, and being able to do the same tasks with high quality. Locus Origin bots are already known for being very high-quality,” Belak said. “We want to bring that same ethos to picking.”

“Picking has historically been a field where the claims have been more focused on the return on investment, without understanding the underlying quality,” he continued. “We can do many picks per hour, but what people don’t focus on is how good are those picks.”

Locus’ team wants to focus on avoiding product damage, double picks, and misspicks, noted Belak. They aren’t often talked about when advertising a robot, but they can eat into a customer’s costs quickly, he added. “Once they have the quality down, then they can worry about increasing speed,” Balak said.

What’s holding back robotic picking?

Locus’ NeuraGrasp can grasp items that were previously difficult to pick, such as porous polybags. | Source: Locus Robotics

Two roadblocks are still hindering the industry, claimed Belak: the development of AI and giving robots a sense of touch. The industry is good at building fancy hands or electromechanical structures, he said. But, when it comes to pinch grasping, the intelligence is still lagging behind.

“[The challenge] is 100% the proprioception and the data metrics and the feedback mechanisms that are there to actually make these hands do things,” Belak said.

This shouldn’t come as a surprise. The robotics industry has raked in millions of dollars of funding in recent years to build a robust physical AI system for robots. And the reality is, human brains evolved over billions of years. Some companies are trying to close this gap by generating as much data as possible, but when you do that, you start to notice the lack of tactile sensing.

“There is one piece of the physical system which is missing, which is the sense of touch on the robots, and particularly robust, reliable touch that doesn’t degrade after very limited usage. That stuff is really tough to simulate or to have the data generated,” Belak said. “I don’t think that simulated data is going to help with this problem very much.”

Nexera does currently use a sense of touch, and it is interested in advancing that in the future. While Locus is still early in its journey with Array, Belak said the company’s manipulation roadmap doesn’t stop with Array.

“Robotic manipulation in general — whether it’s Array, whether it’s other versions of the technology, whether it’s on picking benches, whatever it may be — we have identified that as a pillar of innovation that we want to be exceptional at,” he said.

item.title: Teradyne Robotics ramps up fight against cobot copycats
item.dc:creator: Steve Crowe
item.description:
Teradyne Robotics sued cobot maker JAKA over alleged patent infringement, marking its second battle with a Chinese cobot company in 2026.

The post Teradyne Robotics ramps up fight against cobot copycats appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
If imitation is the sincerest form of flattery, Teradyne Robotics has had enough compliments for one year.

Teradyne Robotics, the parent company of cobot arm maker Universal Robots, has filed a patent infringement lawsuit against a German subsidiary of Chinese robotics company JAKA. The case alleges that JAKA infringed patents covering both hardware and software used in Universal Robots’ collaborative robots.

The lawsuit is Teradyne Robotics’ second major case involving a Chinese robotics company in Europe this year. In February 2026, the company sued Elite Robots’ German subsidiary over alleged copyright infringement.

In April, the Regional Court of Hamburg issued a preliminary injunction prohibiting Elite Robots Germany from offering the disputed software and products containing it in Germany. The case is still ongoing.

The JAKA case is different. “This is a patent case where the other one was about copyright,” David Brandt, vice president of research and development and chief technology officer at Universal Robots, told The Robot Report. “It’s multiple patents this time, and they cover both significant hardware and software aspects of our products.”

Teradyne spots cobot similarities

According to Brandt, Teradyne Robotics became interested in JAKA‘s products after noticing similarities between the two companies’ force- and power-limited robot arms.

“Our robots and the robots of JAKA look quite alike,” Brandt said. “We then chose to acquire one of the robots and take a deeper look at it. Then it became quite obvious that there’s possible patent infringement in this.”

Teradyne Robotics said the lawsuit involves a range of JAKA collaborative robots marketed in the European Union. The company filed the case with the Unified Patent Court (UPC) Local Division in Copenhagen because alleged acts of infringement occurred in Denmark and other EU member states.

EU ruling has broad implications

A ruling from the UPC could have broad geographic implications. According to Teradyne Robotics, a ruling could take effect across 17 of the 18 EU member states participating in the UPC, as well as in certain countries outside the UPC Agreement, including the U.K. and Spain.

The Robot Report reached out to JAKA for comment, but did not hear back at press time.

“This case is another clear demonstration that Teradyne Robotics will enforce its patents and intellectual property (IP) rights against what we consider to be illegal and unfair copying and infringement, across both hardware and software,” stated Teradyne Robotics Group President Jean-Pierre Hathout.

“We cannot and will not accept companies that unlawfully copy protected technologies, and we are resolute in safeguarding our IP so customers can continue to have innovative automation solutions that meet the highest standards for safety and compliance,” he added.

UR Series cobots from Universal Robots.

Comparing cobot portfolios

The dispute puts two collaborative robot portfolios under the microscope. Universal Robots currently divides its robot arms primarily between its UR Series and e-Series. The UR Series includes the UR8 Long, UR15, UR18, UR20 and UR30. Payloads range from 10 kg on the UR8 Long to 35 kg on the UR30, while reach extends to 1,750 mm on the UR8 Long and UR20.

The e-Series is aimed at more compact and general-purpose automation. It currently consists of the UR3e, UR7e, UR12e and UR16e. Payloads range from 3 kg to 16 kg, with reaches from 500 mm to 1,300 mm.

JAKA’s portfolio is similarly extensive. Its current lineup includes the Zu, Pro, S, AL, A and Mini series, along with the MiniCobo. The Zu family includes the Zu3, Zu5, Zu7, Zu12, Zu18, Zu20 and Zu30. The Pro family includes the Pro5, Pro12 and Pro16.

The Zu series is JAKA’s broad general-purpose cobot family. For example, the Zu5 offers a 5-kg payload and 954-mm reach, while the Zu12 carries 12 kg to a 1,327-mm working radius and the Zu18 carries 18 kg to 1,073 mm.

The Pro series is designed for more demanding environments and carries an IP68 rating. It includes the Pro5, Pro12 and Pro16, with payloads of 5, 12 and 16 kg, respectively. The Pro16 offers a 1,713-mm reach and is positioned for applications including palletizing, machine tending, polishing, grinding, and welding.

JAKA’s cobot lineup.

Lawsuit is not about China, says Teradyne

Brandt emphasized that Teradyne’s decision was not driven by JAKA’s Chinese ownership. “To us, it’s not about China,” he said. “It’s about other companies copying stuff that we designed, whether they’re Chinese or not.”

Teradyne Robotics has long maintained a large intellectual property portfolio covering its robot technology. Brandt said the company uses patents, copyrights and trade-secret protections, but acknowledged the fundamental difficulty of protecting robots once they are commercially available.

“You have to build the robot and ship it to a customer to have a robot,” he said. “And, of course, some competitor can buy the robot, take it apart, and look at how we design stuff.”

“We welcome competition and we think competition is healthy,” added Brandt. “But we have a competition where we make big investments in creating what we believe is a great product, having good quality, having a very safe product, a lot of investment going into that. It’s quite expensive to develop such a product, and then having another company simply steal your innovations and copying it. That’s where we’re trying to put our foot down.”

Universal Robots wants JAKA to stop

Brandt said Teradyne’s primary objective isn’t financial compensation. “Ideally, we would like them to stop copying and infringing our IP,” he said. “This is not predominantly for getting money out of JAKA. This is more to send a very clear signal that they need to stop copying our products.”

Brandt also sees a potential safety issue. Universal Robots helped establish the market for collaborative robots designed to operate in proximity to people, subject to appropriate risk assessment and safety measures. Brandt said the proliferation of copycat products that don’t meet the same standards could create risks beyond the companies involved in this dispute.

“If they are not as safe as they should be, and in the worst-case scenario lead to somebody getting seriously hurt by these products, there’s of course a risk that this could reflect badly on the entire industry,” he said.

That could lead regulators and workplace-safety authorities to view collaborative robots more broadly as a safety problem, Brandt said.

“So we are concerned,” he said. “Mostly, of course, we’re concerned about people getting hurt. But there’s also, of course, a business side to that problem.”

Competition in the cobot market

Teradyne Robotics’ two lawsuits underscore the competitive nature of the collaborative robot market. Universal Robots has sold more than 100,000 cobots and has spent more than a decade building an ecosystem around its robot arms, software, and accessories.

Teradyne Robotics generated $100 million in revenue in Q2 2026. The $100 million in quarterly revenue is an increase from the $91 million that its made in Q1 2026.

The North Reading, Mass.-based company marked its fifth consecutive quarter of growth. It also reported 33% year-over-year revenue growth from Q2 2025, when it made $75 million. Most of the $100 million came from Universal Robots, while the rest was generated by its AMR subsidiary Mobile Industrial Robots (MiR).

At the same time, the market has attracted an expanding number of competitors, including companies from China offering cobots at aggressive price points. Brandt said that trend is not necessarily bad for Universal Robots.

“The global market is growing,” he said. “There are just more companies trying to do the same thing, so in that respect, of course, the competition is heating up.”

The problem, in Teradyne Robotics’ view, is where competition crosses into alleged copying of protected technology.

And Brandt suggested that JAKA may not be the last company that Teradyne Robotics challenges. “We do not see this as a one-time thing,” he said. “We are dedicated to aggressively protecting our IP, and JAKA is not the only robot out there that looks suspiciously like ours.”

item.title: NSF to invest $90M into three new technology centers, including one focused on robotics
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
One of the new NSF funded centers will be the Center for Human and Robot Co-Adaptation, led by The University of Texas at Austin.

The post NSF to invest $90M into three new technology centers, including one focused on robotics appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Science and Technology Centers focus on building sustained partnerships across universities, industry, and government and accelerating the use of new ideas and technologies for scientific discovery. | Sources: NSF, left to right: Indiana University, Bloomington; Michigan State University College of Engineering; Brian Scassellati and Kayla Matheus, Yale University

The U.S. National Science Foundation yesterday said it is investing $90 million over five years to support three new Science and Technology Centers, or NSF STCs. The NSF will allocate $6 million annually for an initial five-year period to each of the three centers.

After the first five years, the centers will have the opportunity to compete for up to five additional years of support. The foundation said the centers will advance American leadership in science and technology, strengthen the nation’s STEM workforce, and accelerate innovation in a variety of fields, including AI and robotics.

“Maintaining the United States’ leadership in science and technology requires bold research, strong partnerships, and a skilled workforce,” stated Brian Stone, who is performing the duties of the NSF director. “As advances in foundational science and technology open new possibilities, these Science and Technology Centers will help American researchers seize those opportunities, accelerate scientific discovery, and develop the talent and technologies needed to turn innovation into solutions that benefit the American people.”

Austin center will focus on human-robot collaboration

One of the new centers will be the Center for Human and Robot Co-Adaptation, led by The University of Texas at Austin. This center will study how people and robots can securely and effectively adapt to one another as service and assistive robots become more common in homes, hospitals, workplaces, and public spaces.

Researchers at the center will combine robotics, AI, and human factors to develop new methods that help robots with embodied intelligence learn from people, understand their needs and preferences, and then adapt physically and cognitively to changing environments and different people. The center aims to advance secure, useful robotic technologies that can support independent living, healthcare, and other human-centered services.

The other two centers include the Center for Transformative Explorations in Multi-Physics and Engineering of Scientific Turbulence (TEMPEST), led by Michigan State University, and the Center for Genome Intelligence Engineering (GENIE), led by Northwestern University.

More about the NSF STC program

Since its inception in 1987, the NSF STC program has driven the emergence of new fields of discovery, catalyzed strong partnerships, advanced breakthrough technologies, sparked numerous start-up companies, and trained generations of researchers and innovators.

The program supports large-scale, transformational research that opens new areas of discovery and drives technological innovation. By combining expertise across organizations and partnering with industry and other groups, STCs tackle complex, high-risk challenges in foundational research and help move promising ideas toward real-world benefits.

The NSF added that the centers will strengthen the nation’s scientific and technical workforce by providing students and early-career researchers with hands-on experience in emerging fields. The class of 2026 STCs will focus on strengthening foundational research, advancing critical and emerging technologies, developing the workforce, and translating discoveries into technological advances and national benefits.
